source_title: Regulation of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles; Law Enforcement Acquisition, Warrant, and Weaponization Restrictions
citation: 25 M.R.S. §4501 (Title 25, Part 12, Chapter 551; enacted PL 2015, c. 307, §1, NEW; no subsequent amendment recorded)
effective_date: 2015 (exact effective date not independently re-derived from the 2015 session adjournment calendar in this pass; enacted by PL 2015, c. 307, §1)

uas_topic: Law-enforcement UAS acquisition approval, warrant requirement for criminal investigations, weaponization ban, free-speech-surveillance ban, and mandatory minimum-standards framework (privacy/surveillance, law enforcement)
regulated_party: State and local law enforcement agencies (does not regulate private or commercial UAS operators)
regulated_activity: Acquisition and operation of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) by a law enforcement agency, including criminal-investigation use, weaponized use, and surveillance of persons peacefully exercising free-speech/assembly rights
requirement_type: Prohibition (weaponized use; free-speech surveillance; use before adopting standards; warrantless criminal-investigation use) combined with an acquisition-approval and minimum-standards mandate
permit_or_approval_required: No public/commercial permit process; requires governing-body (or, for a state agency, the commissioner's) approval for a law enforcement agency's own UAV acquisition, and a warrant for criminal-investigation use absent a recognized constitutional exception

aec_relevance: Indirect — relevant context for AEC firms partnering with or contracting to Maine law-enforcement/public-safety agencies (e.g., search-and-rescue mapping, disaster documentation), and for understanding the statutory baseline that followed a 2013 gubernatorial veto and executive order (see ME-008)
summary: 25 M.R.S. §4501 (enacted 2015) governs law enforcement agency acquisition and operation of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), defined as an aircraft operated without a physical human presence that is capable of audio or visual surveillance. Acquisition requires approval of the governing body overseeing the agency (or, for a state agency, the commissioner). Absent a recognized constitutional warrant exception, a law enforcement agency may not use a UAV for criminal investigations without a warrant; UAVs may be used without a warrant for search-and-rescue, training, and non-investigative purposes such as accident, fire, or storm-damage documentation. A weaponized UAV may never be used, or its use facilitated, by state or local law enforcement. UAVs may not be used to surveil persons peacefully exercising free-speech/assembly rights. The Board of Trustees of the Maine Criminal Justice Academy, with the Attorney General, must set minimum written-policy standards (training, prior authorization, data-retention/destruction, altitude/speed limits, statistical reporting), and the Commissioner of Public Safety must report annual UAV-deployment statistics to the Legislature.

summary: 12 M.R.S. §11216 makes it unlawful for a person, on the ground or airborne, to use an aircraft to aid or assist in hunting bear, deer, or moose. Title 12 §10001(1) defines "aircraft" generically as "a machine or device designed for flight," without reference to human occupancy. MDIFW's official published FAQ states this definition — and the statute's prohibition — applies to drones: "Radio controlled helicopters and airplanes are machines or devices that are designed for flight and, therefore, are aircraft as defined in statute," and that using a drone to scout a ridge for deer, push a bear, or locate a moose (including a wounded animal) for hunting purposes violates §11216. A violation without the taking of game is a civil violation (fine of $100-$500); a violation resulting in the taking of a bear, deer, or moose is a Class E crime with a mandatory minimum $500 fine, and repeat civil violations (3 or more within 5 years) escalate to a Class E crime.

regulated_activity: Intentionally or knowingly flying a drone over the premises of a correctional facility or jail at or below 400 feet above ground, landing a drone on the premises, or flying a drone from the premises, without authorization

summary: 17-A M.R.S. §761, enacted by PL 2026, c. 689 (approved April 13, 2026), makes it a civil violation (fine of not less than $500) for a person to intentionally or knowingly fly a drone over the premises of a correctional facility or jail at or below 400 feet above ground, land a drone on the premises, or fly a drone from the premises; a repeat violation (including a substantially similar out-of-state adjudication) is a Class D crime. "Drone" is defined broadly to include an unmanned aircraft system, unmanned aerial vehicle, remotely piloted aircraft system, or micro air vehicle. The section does not apply to a law enforcement officer, corrections officer, or corrections supervisor performing official duty, or to another person acting in the course of employment as approved by the facility's chief administrative officer or the jail administrator. Holding a valid FAA remote pilot certificate or otherwise being permitted to operate under FAA regulations is expressly not a defense to prosecution under this section.

summary: Maine is a strong home-rule state: 30-A M.R.S. §3001 authorizes a municipality to adopt an ordinance exercising any power the Legislature could confer on it that is not expressly or by clear implication denied, with a rebuttable presumption of validity, liberal construction, and a rule that the Legislature is not held to have implicitly denied a municipal power unless the ordinance would frustrate the purpose of a state law. No Maine statute expressly preempting local UAS/drone ordinances, and no Maine statute expressly reserving UAS regulation exclusively to the state (comparable to Louisiana's La. R.S. 2:2), was located during this research pass. This means Maine's state UAS statutes (25 M.R.S. §4501; 12 M.R.S. §11216; 17-A M.R.S. §761) operate as a state-level floor, and individual Maine municipalities retain general home-rule authority to adopt their own UAS-related ordinances unless a specific ordinance is found to frustrate a state law's purpose — a fact-specific standard not tested by any UAS-specific Maine court decision located in this pass.

summary: No Maine state-court decision, Attorney General opinion, or currently operative gubernatorial executive order directly and dispositively addressing UAS regulation was located in this research pass. In 2013, the Legislature passed LD 236 (126th Legislature), which would have required a warrant for law-enforcement UAV surveillance; Governor Paul LePage vetoed it, stating Maine did not have a "drone problem," and the veto was not overridden. LePage then issued an executive order (eff. Aug. 10, 2013) directing the Commissioner of Public Safety to issue, by Feb. 1, 2014, an interim policy governing state law-enforcement UAV use; that order and any resulting interim policy were superseded when the Legislature enacted the current controlling statute, 25 M.R.S. §4501, in 2015 (ME-001). Separately, LD 2144 (129th Legislature, "An Act to Protect Maine Residents from Stalking and Unauthorized Surveillance by Use of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle") would have added explicit UAV language to the stalking statute's "course of conduct" definition (17-A §210-A) and created a new UAV-specific violation-of-privacy provision (a 400-foot altitude threshold over a private place, 17-A §511); per the bill's official legislature.maine.gov status page, it was referred to the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, carried over, never reported out, and "Died Upon Conclusion of the 129th Legislature" on Nov. 16, 2020 — it was never enacted. No enacted Maine statute imposing a state-agency UAS procurement or country-of-origin restriction was located.

notes: MATERIAL FINDING — BILL/STATUTE CURRENCY CORRECTION: at least one secondary search-result summary encountered in this research pass described Maine's stalking statute's "course of conduct" definition as currently including express "use of an unmanned aerial vehicle" language, matching LD 2144's proposed (but never enacted) amendment almost verbatim. The current codified 17-A §210-A(2)(A), as most recently amended by PL 2023, c. 519, §2 (which repealed and replaced the definition), reads only "by any action, method, device or means" — generic language that would likely encompass a drone in practice but no longer contains the explicit "unmanned aerial vehicle" phrase — and 17-A §511 (violation of privacy) contains no UAV-specific provision or 400-foot altitude threshold at all. This is the same enacted-vs-died-in-committee pattern flagged in this program's Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, and Louisiana research; AEC firms and counsel should not rely on any secondary source describing Maine's stalking or privacy statutes as containing UAV-specific language without independently confirming current codified text via legislature.maine.gov.
